sections.b:
Most of Jude 4–18 has a counterpart in 2 Peter 2:1–3:3, usually in the same order:

  • Intruders slip in and deny the Master (Jude 4; 2 Peter 2:1–3)
  • Angels held in darkness for judgment (Jude 6; 2 Peter 2:4)
  • Sodom and Gomorrah as an example (Jude 7; 2 Peter 2:6)
  • They defile the flesh, despise authority and slander glorious ones (Jude 8; 2 Peter 2:10)
  • Angels do not bring a slanderous judgment (Jude 9; 2 Peter 2:11)
  • Like animals without reason (Jude 10; 2 Peter 2:12)
  • Balaam's error, for pay (Jude 11; 2 Peter 2:15–16)
  • Blots at your feasts; waterless clouds or springs; darkness reserved (Jude 12–13; 2 Peter 2:13, 17)
  • Puffed-up words (Jude 16; 2 Peter 2:18)
  • Remember the apostles; mockers in the last time (Jude 17–18; 2 Peter 3:2–3)

Most scholars: 2 Peter used Jude. Jude's version is shorter, tighter and more vivid. 2 Peter drops Jude's quotations from 1 Enoch and the Assumption of Moses and makes the angels' example vaguer, which is easy to explain if a later writer was wary of those books, and hard to explain the other way. 2 Peter also puts the examples in Old Testament order (angels, flood, Sodom) and adds hopeful examples (Noah, Lot). A minority: Jude used 2 Peter. Luther thought Jude looked like a summary of 2 Peter, and some later scholars held that Jude 17–18 quotes 2 Peter 3:3. Others: a shared source. Both drew on common preaching against false teachers. Whichever view is right, the two letters were already linked in the early church, and both were among the "disputed" books.

common: 2 Peter borrowed most of its second chapter from Jude.
uncommon: Jude summarized 2 Peter, and Jude 17–18 quotes 2 Peter 3:3 as the words of an apostle.

sections.b: The writer of Jude calls himself "a slave of Jesus Christ and a brother of James" (Jude 1). The only James who needed no further description was James of Jerusalem, so most readers, ancient and modern, take Jude to be the Judas of Mark 6:3. That he calls himself Jesus's "servant" rather than his brother is often read as humility. Paul's note that "the brothers of the Lord" traveled with their wives (1 Corinthians 9:5) suggests Jude was a traveling missionary.

Hegesippus, a Christian writer of the 100s quoted by Eusebius (Church History 3.19–20), tells that two grandsons of Jude, "the Lord's brother according to the flesh," were brought before the emperor Domitian because they were descendants of David. They showed him their hands, calloused from farm work, and said Christ's kingdom was heavenly, not earthly; he let them go, and they became leaders in the churches. Relatives of Jesus (Greek desposynoi, "those of the Master") remained respected in Palestinian Christianity for generations.

common: Jude the letter writer was a younger half-brother of Jesus.
uncommon: Jude was the apostle Judas son of James (Luke 6:16), not Jesus's brother. This was the older Western identification, Jude Thaddeus, but Jude 17 seems to set the writer apart from the apostles.

sections.b: Jude 14–15 quotes 1 Enoch 1:9, the opening oracle of the Book of the Watchers, introduced with the book's own title for Enoch, "the seventh from Adam" (1 Enoch 60:8). Jude calls it prophecy. He also draws on 1 Enoch's story of the Watchers for Jude 6 and on its picture of disobedient stars for Jude 13. 1 Enoch 1:9 itself echoes Deuteronomy 33:2, and Jude adds "the Lord," so that the coming of God becomes the coming of Jesus.

Because Jude quotes Enoch, early Christians argued about both books. Tertullian (about AD 200) defended 1 Enoch's authority partly because "Enoch has a witness in the apostle Jude." Jerome (AD 392) reports that many rejected Jude because it quotes an apocryphal book. In the end Jude was kept and 1 Enoch was dropped in most churches, except the Ethiopian Orthodox, whose Bible still includes it.

common: Jude quoting Enoch does not make 1 Enoch Scripture, any more than Paul quoting Greek poets makes them Scripture.
uncommon: Jude treated 1 Enoch as inspired prophecy, so the church should at least read it with respect, as the Ethiopian church does.

sections.b: "The angels who did not keep to their own rank, but deserted the dwelling that was theirs, he has kept in everlasting chains down in the gloom, for the judgment of the great day" (Jude 6). The wording follows 1 Enoch 10–15: the Watchers left "the high, holy heaven," were bound in darkness, and await the great day of judgment. Jude places them between Israel in the wilderness and Sodom, and says Sodom sinned "like these" (Jude 7), going after "other flesh," the reverse of the angels' crossing. In Jude 13 the intruders are "wandering stars" whose gloom is "kept," the angels' own fate. Behind both stands Isaiah 24:21–22, where the host of heaven is shut up in a pit and punished "after many days." 2 Peter 2:4 shortens the example and says God threw them into Tartarus.
sections.refs: Jude 6–7; Jude 13; 2 Peter 2:4; Genesis 6:1–4; Isaiah 24:21–22; 1 Peter 3:19–20

common: Jude 6 describes Satan's angels falling before the creation of the world.
Many commentators on 1 Peter (Selwyn, Dalton, Elliott, Achtemeier) take the "spirits in prison" of 1 Peter 3:19 to be the same bound angels as Jude 6, to whom the risen Christ announced his victory.
uncommon: Between his death and resurrection Christ went down to Hades and preached to the human dead, offering them a chance to repent.

sections.b: Jude 7 sets Sodom and Gomorrah beside the angels of Jude 6. Like them, Sodom "gave themselves to sexual immorality and went after other flesh," and now the cities "are set out as an example," undergoing "the punishment of eternal fire." Many commentators think "other flesh" refers to the attempt on Lot's angel guests (Genesis 19:1–11), the mirror image of angels taking human wives; the traditional reading takes it as same-sex desire, and some see both. 2 Peter 2:6–8 repeats the example and adds Lot as one God rescued.

common: Jude 7 shows that Sodom's sin was homosexuality.
uncommon: Sodom's "other flesh" was angelic flesh: the men of Sodom, like the Watchers, tried to cross the line between heaven and earth.

sections.b: Jude 11 begins its trio of Old Testament rebels with Cain. Jewish tradition by then had made Cain more than a murderer. In the Palestinian Targums on Genesis 4:8 he says, "There is no judgment, no judge, no world to come," and Josephus describes him as greedy and a teacher of wickedness. That fits Jude's intruders: people who deny judgment and lead others astray. Jude also treats Cain as the first of a series of ever bolder rebels, ending with Korah.

Jude 11 ends its three woes with Korah, who challenged the authority of Moses and Aaron and was swallowed by the earth (Numbers 16). Jude's word antilogia, "talking back," fits teachers who "set aside lordship" (Jude 8). The past tense, "they perished," treats their fate as already sealed. The Mishnah (Avot 5:17; 5:20 in some editions) also uses Korah as the model of a dispute "not for the sake of heaven."

Jude 9 tells that "Michael the archangel was arguing with the devil, disputing about the body of Moses," and said only, "The Lord rebuke you!" The story is not in the Old Testament. Origen and other early writers say it came from the Assumption of Moses. A Jewish work about Moses's last words survives in one incomplete Latin manuscript (usually called the Testament of Moses), and its lost ending may have contained the scene. Later Christian sources say the devil claimed the body because Moses had killed an Egyptian.

uncommon: Michael fought for Moses's body because God planned to raise it, so Moses could appear with Elijah at the transfiguration (Matthew 17:3).

sections.h: Michael and the devil in Jude
sections.b: In Jude 9 the archangel Michael argues with the devil over the body of Moses. Even he "did not dare to bring a slanderous judgment" against the devil, but left the verdict to God with the words of Zechariah 3:2, "The Lord rebuke you!" Jude's point is about authority: the intruders casually insult angels, while the greatest angel would not presume to pass sentence even on the devil. This is the only place the Bible calls Michael "the archangel" by name.

Jude's short letter mentions angels in four ways: the angels who left their place and are held in darkness (Jude 6); the "glorious ones" the intruders slander (Jude 8); Michael, who would not slander even the devil (Jude 9); and the "holy ones by the tens of thousands" who come with the Lord in Enoch's prophecy (Jude 14). Jude shares the Jewish belief that angels have assigned ranks (archē, "rank, domain") and guard the order of creation.

"For pay they have thrown themselves into Balaam's error" (Jude 11). Jude stresses Balaam's greed: he was a prophet for hire. Numbers 31:16 blames Balaam's advice for Israel's sin with the women of Moab and their gods at Peor, so "Balaam's error" also suggests leading God's people into sexual sin and idolatry, which is how Revelation 2:14 uses his name. 2 Peter 2:15–16 expands Jude's line with the story of the talking donkey.

Jude quotes 1 Enoch 1:9 as Enoch's prophecy (Jude 14–15), and tells a story about Michael and Moses that early writers traced to the Assumption of Moses (Jude 9). He also uses 1 Enoch's Watcher story (Jude 6) and its disobedient stars (Jude 13). Christians have explained this in three main ways: Jude regarded these books as true prophecy; Jude quoted true statements from books he did not regard as Scripture; or Jude used books his readers respected to make his point. Jude is the New Testament book that most openly uses Jewish writings outside the Hebrew Bible.

common: Quoting a book is not the same as calling it Scripture.
uncommon: Jude's use of Enoch shows that the edges of the Bible were not yet fixed in the first century, so the question "Is this Scripture?" may not have been Jude's question at all.

sections.b: Jude was known early: the Muratorian list (probably late 100s) accepts it, and Clement of Alexandria, Tertullian and Origen quote it. But Eusebius (about 325) lists it among the "disputed" books, and Jerome says many rejected it because it quotes 1 Enoch. The original Syriac Bible left it out. Martin Luther, in 1522, placed Jude with Hebrews, James and Revelation at the end of his New Testament, saying it seemed to be an extract from 2 Peter and used stories found nowhere in Scripture. All major churches today include it.

Jude never says what the intruders taught. He describes how they lived and spoke. They "slipped in among you without being noticed" (Jude 4), probably as traveling teachers. They claimed visions ("dreamers," Jude 8), turned grace into license (Jude 4), rejected authority and mocked angels (Jude 8–10), ate at the church's love feasts while looking out for themselves (Jude 12), flattered people for gain (Jude 16), and divided the church into the "spiritual" and the rest (Jude 19). Scholars have called them antinomians (people "against law"), early Gnostics, or simply charismatic libertines. Jude's answer is double: judgment for the teachers, mercy for those they unsettle (Jude 22–23).

uncommon: Jude's opponents were not teaching a new doctrine at all; they were Paul's message of freedom taken to an extreme (compare 1 Corinthians 6:12).

sections.b: Jude's intruders "turn the grace of our God into shameless self-indulgence" (Jude 4). They kept the language of grace but treated forgiveness as permission. Jude's answer is not less grace but more: the letter opens and closes with God's keeping power (Jude 1, 24) and urges the readers to "Keep yourselves in God's love" (Jude 21). Grace that changes nothing is, to Jude, a way of disowning "our only Master and Lord."

Jude 12 gives the earliest use of "love feasts" (agapai) for the church's shared meal. The intruders are "sunken rocks" there, eating "without fear." The danger is that the meal of fellowship, where the Lord's Supper was shared, became the place where the intruders did their damage. 2 Peter 2:13 has a similar line, and some manuscripts there read "love feasts" too.

Jude reminds his readers that the apostles "kept telling you, 'In the last time there will be mockers who live by their own ungodly desires'" (Jude 18). He then applies it: "These people draw dividing lines" (Jude 19). Like other New Testament writers, Jude believes he is living in the last time already. 2 Peter 3:3–4 repeats the saying and adds that the mockers ask, "Where is the promise of his coming?"

sections.h: Those who have the Spirit, and those who don't
sections.b: Jude's intruders claimed to be the spiritual ones, but Jude calls them "merely natural" (psychikoi) people who "lack the Spirit" (Jude 19). In contrast, the readers "pray in the Holy Spirit" (Jude 20). Jude's closing instructions name the Spirit, the love of God, and the mercy of the Lord Jesus Christ together (Jude 20–21), an early example of Father, Son and Spirit named side by side.

uncommon: "Pray in the Holy Spirit" in Jude 20 means praying in tongues.

sections.b: Jude wishes his readers mercy (Jude 2), tells them to look forward to "the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ" at his coming (Jude 21), and then tells them to show mercy, twice, to people being pulled away (Jude 22–23). A letter that speaks so harshly of the intruders ends with mercy for those they have unsettled. The mercy is careful: "with fear," hating the stained clothing while rescuing the person.

Jude, only 25 verses long, has two of the hardest textual problems in the New Testament. In Jude 5, the oldest manuscripts are split between "Jesus," "the Lord," "God," and Papyrus 72's "God Christ" as the one who saved Israel from Egypt; the newest critical editions (NA28 and the Editio Critica Maior) print "Jesus." In Jude 22–23, the manuscripts give two groups or three, and different verbs ("have mercy," "correct," "snatch"). Papyrus 72, copied around AD 300, is the oldest complete copy of Jude, and it often stands alone. Papyrus 78, a small fragment of Jude 4–8, is from about the same time.

Jude 14–15 quotes 1 Enoch 1:9 in its own form: "Look! The Lord has come with his holy ones by the tens of thousands, to carry out judgment on everyone" (Jude 14–15). Enoch itself reads, "Look! He has come with ten thousands of holy ones to carry out judgment on all" (1 Enoch 1:9). Jude reads Enoch's coming of God as the coming of the Lord Jesus, with angels, as Jesus himself describes (Matthew 25:31). The readers "look forward to the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ" (Jude 21) and the God who will "set you in front of his glory" (Jude 24).

sections.b: Jude's first warning is the Exodus generation: "Jesus saved a people out of the land of Egypt, and later destroyed those who did not believe" (Jude 5). Like 1 Corinthians 10:1–12 and Hebrews 3–4, Jude uses the wilderness as a warning: rescue at the start does not guarantee arrival. If "Jesus" is the original reading, Jude sees Christ himself as the rescuer in the Exodus. The "grumblers" of Jude 16 recall the same generation.

sections.h: Eternal fire and darkness in Jude
sections.b: Jude uses two pictures of final punishment side by side: "the punishment of eternal fire" seen in Sodom (Jude 7) and "the gloom of darkness... kept forever" (Jude 13; compare Jude 6). Some interpreters argue that fire and darkness cannot both be literal at once, so both are pictures of a real ruin; others answer that two images can describe one reality. Traditionalists read Jude 7 as describing unending punishment; conditionalists note that Sodom's fire is "eternal" in its result, total destruction.
